scenes.tts: In 1850, Helmholtz timed a nerve signal in a frog's leg. The signal ran at a few tens of metres per second, about the speed of a car on a motorway. So a nerve signal has a finite speed. What route does it take, from a sense organ to a muscle?
scenes.visual: electric shock chip and muscle chip joined by a nerve bar; a dot crosses it slowly; speed and motorway labels; then the bar becomes a question-mark route from sense organ to muscle
scenes.narration: In 1850, Helmholtz timed a nerve signal in a frog's leg. The signal ran at a few tens of metres per second, about the speed of a car on a motorway. So a nerve signal has a finite speed. What route does it take, from a sense organ to a muscle?

scenes.tts: The route is built from neurons, which are nerve cells. In a typical vertebrate motor neuron, the dendrites receive signals. The cell body gathers that input. A single long axon carries the signal away. Axon terminals at its far end pass the signal on. The signal on the axon is an impulse. It is all or none: it fires at full size, or not at all. At most synapses, the terminal releases a chemical that crosses a narrow gap to the next cell.
scenes.visual: a motor neuron as labelled blocks; parts appear as named; an impulse dot runs down the axon; chemical dots cross the gap to the next cell

scenes.tts: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. Its pathway is the reflex arc, which has five parts. A receptor detects the stimulus. A sensory neuron carries it into the central nervous system. An integrating centre sits there. A motor neuron carries the output out. The effector, a muscle or a gland, responds.
scenes.visual: the five parts appear one by one around a central nervous system box, and the signal dot runs the whole arc
scenes.narration: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. Its pathway is the reflex arc, which has five parts. A receptor detects the stimulus. A sensory neuron carries it into the central nervous system. An integrating centre sits there. A motor neuron carries the output out. The effector, a muscle or a gland, responds.

scenes.tts: Take the knee jerk in humans. A tap on the tendon below the kneecap stretches the quadriceps muscle. Stretch receptors there, the muscle spindles, fire. Their sensory fibres enter the spinal cord and synapse directly on the motor neurons of the same quadriceps. Those neurons make the muscle contract, and the leg kicks. This direct path has one synapse in the cord, so it is monosynaptic.
scenes.visual: the arc labelled for the knee jerk: tap, muscle spindle, one synapse node in the cord, quadriceps; the signal runs through and the effector flashes
scenes.narration: Take the knee jerk in humans. A tap on the tendon below the kneecap stretches the quadriceps muscle. Stretch receptors there, the muscle spindles, fire. scenes.tts: Now the withdrawal reflex, pulling your foot away from a tack. It works through interneurons from the start. The pain-sensing endings of sensory neurons in the skin fire. Those sensory neurons excite interneurons in the spinal cord. The interneurons activate motor neurons of the flexor muscles, and the limb lifts. Other interneurons inhibit the opposing extensor muscles.
scenes.visual: the arc labelled for the withdrawal reflex: pain receptors, interneuron chips inside the cord, flexor muscles excited, extensor muscles inhibited

scenes.tts: The knee jerk is a somatic reflex, because its effector is skeletal muscle. Somatic does not mean voluntary. Its direct path has one synapse, yet interneurons also quiet the opposing hamstring muscles. Many other reflexes use interneurons. So keep this rule. Trace any reflex as five parts: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating centre, motor neuron, and effector.
scenes.visual: the five parts in a row; knee jerk and interneuron variants beneath; somatic note on the effector; the signal runs the row
